keyVerseText: And when he was come to the other side into the country of the Gergesenes, there met him two possessed with devils, coming out of the tombs, exceeding fierce, so that no man might pass by that way.
rootMeaning: The word μνημεῖον (mnēmeîon) derives from the root μνήμη (mnḗmē), meaning remembrance or memory. This etymological connection highlights that μνημεῖον originally signifies more than just a physical tomb or grave; it is fundamentally a memorial or record that preserves the memory of a person or event. Thus, beyond the common English gloss of 'tomb' or 'sepulchre,' the term carries the deeper sense of a tangible reminder meant to keep something or someone remembered.
usageInScripture: Across its 42 occurrences in Scripture, μνημεῖον is predominantly translated as 'the sepulchre' or 'the tomb,' showing a consistent usage referring to burial places. However, its semantic range includes 'memorial' or 'record,' indicating that it can also mean a monument or cenotaph serving as a remembrance. This dual usage reflects both the physical reality of a burial site and the spiritual or cultural function of memorializing the dead or significant events.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, μνημεῖον reminds believers that physical tombs are not merely places of death but also serve as memorials that testify to the reality of human mortality and the hope of resurrection. In the Christian faith, the tomb of Christ is the ultimate μνημεῖον, a memorial of His death and a signpost to His victory over death. Recognizing this word's original meaning enriches our understanding of how Scripture portrays death and remembrance—not as finality, but as a call to remember God's redemptive work and the promise of eternal life through Christ.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 8:28, the phrase 'coming out of the tombs' uses μνημεῖον to describe the place of the possessed men's confinement after death. This word emphasizes the physical and somber reality of death's domain, from which Jesus' power liberates them. The use of μνημεῖον here underscores the spiritual darkness associated with death and the grave, setting the stage for Christ's authority to bring life and freedom even from the most fearsome places.
